cases.title: The mayor’s announcement

item.description: The mayor appears to announce that summer vacation is being cut by two weeks.

clues.A: An account called CityNewsNow, not the city’s official account.
clues.B: The city’s website and real news outlets have nothing about it.
clues.C: Her lips are slightly out of sync on a few words. Otherwise it’s convincing.
clues.D: It mentions a “new state law” but never names it.
clues.E: Reporters ask the mayor’s office. They say the video is fake.

cases.lesson: Deepfakes of officials spread fast. Check official channels and real news outlets before sharing.

fib.right: Ugh. You called the mayor’s office.
fib.wrong: Gotcha! The mayor never said that. I did.

cases.title: The council meeting photo

item.description: Students hold signs at a city council meeting. A popular comment says “This is obviously AI.”

clues.A: A photographer for the local paper, credited by name.
clues.B: Several people posted photos of the same meeting from different angles.
clues.D: The caption names the meeting date and the issue being discussed.
clues.E: The photographer shares two more shots taken seconds apart.

cases.lesson: Calling something AI can be a trick too. Judge the evidence, not the accusation.

fib.right: Fine. The sign was just bent.
fib.wrong: Ha! Real photo. You believed the comment instead of the evidence.

cases.title: The eyewitness post

item.description: A vivid first-person account of a fire downtown, shared 10,000 times.

clues.A: An account created yesterday, with no photos of its own.
clues.B: The fire department confirms a small fire, but the post’s details, like three trucks and a rescued parrot, appear nowhere else.
clues.C: The writing is vivid and well organized, like a story.
clues.D: It mentions a bakery on that street that closed years ago.
clues.E: Asked for a photo, the account posts a stock image.

cases.lesson: AI can wrap invented details around a real event. Check the details you can verify.

fib.right: Rats. The bakery closed years ago.
fib.wrong: Gotcha! There was a fire. The parrot was my idea.

cases.title: The screen time chart

item.description: In a class debate, a classmate shares a chart showing teen screen time doubling over ten years.

clues.A: It comes from a university research center’s report, linked in the slide.
clues.B: The report on the center’s website has the same chart and a data table.
clues.C: The colors and fonts look like a template.
clues.D: The report says how many teens were surveyed and when.
clues.E: You email the center. They reply explaining how the survey was done.
clues.F: It’s labeled with the report’s name as the source.

cases.lesson: For data, look for the method: who was asked, how many and when.

fib.right: Hmph. You actually read the method.
fib.wrong: Ha! Real data. A template doesn’t make it fake.

cases.title: The vacation photo

item.description: Your classmate Dana posts herself standing in front of the Eiffel Tower.

clues.A: Dana posted it on her own account.
clues.B: A reverse image search finds the background in a stock photo.
clues.C: Shadows on Dana fall to the left. Shadows on the tower fall to the right.
clues.D: Dana can’t name the hotel, the food or anything she did there.
clues.E: You ask about the flight. Dana laughs and says she made it with an app.

cases.lesson: Light and shadows that don’t match are a clue. So is a story with no details.

fib.wrong: Gotcha! Dana never left the city.

cases.title: The perfect performance

item.description: A 14-year-old sings a hard song in perfect pitch.

clues.A: A local music school’s official channel.
clues.B: Her school also posted her singing the same song at a concert.
clues.C: Her voice is so clean it sounds edited.
clues.D: The video names her teacher, the competition and the date.
clues.E: Asked if it was edited, the music school shares the raw recording.

cases.lesson: Talent can look fake. Raw recordings and other performances are evidence.

fib.right: Fine. She really is that good.
fib.wrong: Ha! Real voice. You doubted a real talent.

cases.title: The study guide

item.description: A study guide for the science test, shared in the class group chat.

clues.A: A classmate shared it. He didn’t say where it came from.
clues.B: It’s different from the guide your teacher posted.
clues.C: It’s neatly formatted and confident, but says the Moon is about 384 kilometers from Earth. It’s about 384,000.
clues.D: It covers topics your class never studied and skips two that are on the test.
clues.E: The classmate admits he generated it from the test’s title.

cases.lesson: AI can sound sure and still be wrong. Check facts against your own notes.

fib.right: Rats. You knew how far the Moon is.
fib.wrong: Gotcha! Good luck on that test.

cases.title: The scientist’s interview

item.description: A marine scientist describes a research trip. Her voice has an odd, robotic echo.

clues.B: Her university page lists the interview and her published research.
clues.C: Her voice has a strange robotic echo.
clues.D: She tells a story about the research boat’s engine failing, naming the boat.
clues.E: Listeners ask about the echo. The host says the microphone was faulty.

cases.lesson: Bad audio isn’t proof of AI. Confirm the person exists and the source is real.

fib.right: Bah. It was just a bad microphone.
fib.wrong: Ha! Real scientist. Bad sound isn’t AI.

cases.title: The tutor’s email

item.description: “Ms. Carter, Math Tutor” offers you free help and says she loved your recent math project.

clues.A: The sender’s address is a random string of letters at a free email service.
clues.B: No tutor by that name exists at your school or online.
clues.C: It’s perfectly polite but opens with “Dear Student,” not your name.
clues.D: It praises “your recent math project” but never says which one.
clues.E: You ask which project. The reply repeats the first email word for word, with a link.

cases.lesson: Generic praise, no real details and a link is a common pattern. Show an adult before clicking anything.

cases.title: The neat quiz

item.description: Your English teacher’s quiz has questions that all look the same length and style.

clues.A: Your English teacher handed it out.
clues.C: Every question is the same length with four choices, like a template.
clues.D: The questions use jokes and examples from your class discussions.
clues.E: You ask. She shows you her drafts with crossed-out questions.

cases.lesson: Neat and template-like isn’t proof. Details from your own class are hard for AI to know.

fib.wrong: Ha! Your teacher wrote it. Neat isn’t the same as AI.
